turns.q:
Your response was: "Looked at it. Most of it made sense. One thing didn't — two buttons at the bottom. Went to the wrong one first. Darker one drew my eye. That wasn't the action I needed."

We want to understand what you meant by "went to the wrong one first", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The visual hierarchy is misleading because the "Continue Shopping" button is styled with high contrast (dark background), making it appear more prominent than the primary action.
B) The spatial arrangement is confusing because the secondary action ("Continue Shopping") is placed above the primary action ("Place Order"), contrary to standard checkout flows.
C) The visual hierarchy is misleading because the "Place Order" button is styled with low contrast (light background), making it appear inactive or disabled compared to the other button.
D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
If the "Continue Shopping" button were styled with the same light background as the "Place Order" button, would you still have looked at it first?
turns.a: 'Continue Shopping.' Heavier. More presence. 'Place Order' is the lighter one.

turns.q: If a developer built this layout exactly as shown, how would that visual weight affect someone trying to complete their purchase for the first time?
turns.a: Same. Went to the heavier one first. Had to re-read to sort it out.

turns.q: If that visual weight were corrected so "Place Order" stood out, would you still feel the need to re-read the buttons, or is the current contrast the sole reason for that hesitation?
turns.a: Make it obvious which one is the checkout step. Right now it's the wrong one.

turns.q: If you could rearrange just those two buttons to make the checkout step unmistakable, what specific visual change would you apply to ensure "Place Order" is instantly recognized as the primary action?
turns.a: Ghost 'Continue Shopping' — no fill, border outline or text link only. Give 'Place Order' a solid fill in a high-contrast color. Visual hierarchy then matches the intended UX: primary CTA reads primary, secondary CTA reads secondary. One CSS property change per button. That's the fix.
